analysis.one_liner: Requires no-excuse mail voting and 20-day early voting, with federal funds, for the 2020 pandemic elections.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing: it sat in the Senate Rules Committee from May 13, 2020, until the 116th Congress ended without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The VoteSafe Act would have required every state to offer no-excuse mail-in voting for the 2020 federal elections, with prepaid return envelopes, online ballot requests, signature-cure processes, and secured drop boxes. It would also have required at least 20 days of early in-person voting, including weekends, and required states to follow CDC COVID-19 guidance at polling places, including hazard pay and protective equipment for poll workers. It authorized $5 billion in federal payments to states and local election offices to pay for all of this.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in states without no-excuse mail voting or long early-voting periods, especially people with disabilities, language-minority voters, tribal and rural voters, older voters, and anyone at higher risk from COVID-19. Poll workers would also gain hazard pay and protective equipment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters in restrictive states; disabled, rural, and high-risk voters

how_it_helps.text: Each state would have to mail a prepaid, self-sealing absentee ballot to any registered voter who requests one, allow online ballot requests, count ballots postmarked by Election Day, and provide secured drop boxes starting 45 days before the election [S2][S3].
Voters would get a chance to fix (cure) signature problems before their ballots are discarded, with bipartisan review by at least two election officials before any rejection [S3].
Every state would have to keep early in-person voting open at least 20 days, including one Saturday and one Sunday, with polls open a minimum of 10 hours each day [S2][S3].
States would have to write plans to keep polling places open, provide social distancing, cleaning supplies, and protective equipment, and pay poll workers hazard pay during the pandemic [S2][S3].

The bill directs extra grant money toward voters with disabilities, language-minority voters, American Indian and Alaska Native voters, and rural voters, including accessible ballot-marking technology, tribal polling places, and transportation to polls [S3].

The Election Assistance Commission would pay every state within 30 days, with at least 70 percent of funds passed down to local election offices, and would pay extra to states that had to build new systems to comply [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, which would have covered $5 billion in authorized appropriations, and state and local election offices, which would have borne the operational work of running expanded mail and early voting programs for the 2020 cycle.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and state election offices

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state election rules: it preempts how states run mail voting, early voting, and ballot signature review for federal elections, which supporters of state control of elections objected to as a federal mandate on election administration [S3].

The bill sets a high bar before rejecting a mismatched signature — a ballot counts unless officials unanimously determine beyond a reasonable doubt it is invalid — and places no limit on how many ballots one designated person may return, rules critics said make signature and ballot-chain safeguards weaker than many states had [S3].
The $5 billion was authorized but not appropriated by this bill itself, so states could have been required to comply before Congress separately funded the mandate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the 2020 elections, held during a respiratory pandemic, the bill offered a clear public benefit: giving every voter a safe way to vote by mail while also protecting and expanding in-person options, with federal money attached to cover the cost. The honest objections are that it imposed uniform national rules on election systems states administer themselves, weakened some signature-verification processes, and counted its $5 billion as an authorization rather than a guarantee of funding. Weighing pandemic-era voting access against those costs, the benefit to voters is substantially larger.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to the Rules and Administration Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Kamala Harris introduced the VoteSafe Act of 2020 on May 13, 2020, with 18 cosponsors — 17 Democrats and 1 Independent — all from outside the Republican Party [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration; that was the last action of any kind in the record [S1][S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or any other consideration, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing the bill [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State election officials who did not want federal voting mandates, and Senate leaders who preferred not to hold a vote on national mail-voting standards, were better off because the bill died; voters in states without no-excuse mail voting had to rely on state-level rules for the 2020 election.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State officials resisting federal voting mandates

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Did not bring election or voting legislation to the Senate floor in 2020, and no Senate voting-rights bill reached a vote that session

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent, and no Republican signed on; the bill died without a roll call, so no vote split is recorded.

industries.note: States buying Remote Access Vote-By-Mail systems, ballot-marking devices, and drop boxes would have purchased from these vendors. The public benefit (accessible voting) and vendor revenue run in the same direction here.

The bill would have handed them federal money (at least 70 percent going to local governments) but also imposed new mandatory programs on tight 2020 timelines. Their interest in serving voters runs alongside the public's.
